email.scenario: During today's scheduled consultation hours, a graduate teaching assistant discovers that the reserved seminar room's projector cable is missing. Without it, Friday's course review session for the whole class is at risk.
email.subject: Missing Projector Cable in Room 214 Ahead of Friday's Review Session
bullets: Report that the projector cable in the reserved seminar room is missing.
Request a replacement cable or a loaner unit be sent before Friday.
Ask whether an alternate room could be reserved as a backup in case the cable isn't found.

academicDiscussion.professorPost: This week we're discussing a growing corporate practice: requiring all remote employees to attend a quarterly in-person offsite at company expense. Supporters argue these gatherings rebuild the trust and team cohesion that daily video calls can't fully replace. Critics see them as a costly intrusion on the flexibility remote work was supposed to provide. What do you think? Should companies require this kind of in-person attendance, or should remote employees be free to opt out?

studentPosts.name: Maya
studentPosts.post: I think the quarterly offsite makes sense. Video calls work for updates, but trust builds faster in person — sharing a meal or solving a problem face-to-face does something a screen can't. Since the company covers travel, the real cost to employees is small compared to what a team gains from actually knowing each other.

studentPosts.name: Daniel
studentPosts.post: I get Maya's point about trust, but mandatory travel four times a year isn't really free — it eats into personal time and disrupts caregiving schedules that remote work was supposed to protect. A company that hired people for flexibility shouldn't turn around and require attendance; optional meetups would let cohesion build more naturally.
